questions.question: Walk me through a recent deal you found interesting and why.
questions.answer:
What it tests: Whether you follow the market or only revised for the interview. This is where prepared answers come apart under a second question.
A strong answer contains: One deal you can defend in depth: the strategic logic, roughly what was paid and how it was financed, and one thing you would question about it. Pick a deal in the group's sector if you can.
Red flags: Naming a famous megadeal with no view on it. Also risky: choosing a deal the group actually worked on and getting the facts wrong.

questions.question: How would depreciation going up by 10 affect the 3 statements?
questions.answer:
a. IS
i. EBT would both down by 10
ii. With a 40% tax rate, a 4 dollar tax shield is create because it would be -10 * -.4
iii. The resulting net income would be -6
b. SCF
i. -6 would become the top of the SCF
ii. Add back depreciation of 10 to end up with 4
iii. 4 is the net change in cash
c. BS
i. PPE goes down by 10
ii. Net cash goes up by 4
iii. Net change in assets is -6
iv. B/C net income is -6 the Liabilities and Shareholder’s Equity side is also -6

questions.question: What happens to the 3 statements which prepaid expenses decrease by 10?
questions.answer:
a. IS
i. EBT is down by 10 and NI is thus down by 6
b. SCF
i. Start off at -6 from NI
ii. B/c prepaid expenses is an asset, a decrease in prepaid expenses by 10 leads to an increase in cash flow by 10
iii. Add back 10 in prepaid expenses in the statement of cash flows
iv. Net change in cash becomes 4
c. BS
i. Net cash is up by 4
ii. Prepaid expenses are down by 10
iii. Net change in assets is -6
iv. B/c NI is -6 there’s balance

ii. EBT increases by 20

iv. Net income is 12
b. SCF

ii. Subtract out the gain of 20 from the sale of the asset
iii. CFO is down by 8
iv. In CFI, record entire amount of sale proceeds of 120
v. Net change in cash is 112
c. BS
i. Cash is up by 112
ii. PPE is down by 100 because you no longer have it
iii. Asset side is up by 12
iv. B/c NI is 12, the L+SE side is also 12 and therefore balances

questions.question: Company has NOLs of 100 in DTA line item on BS because it had been unprofitable. Company turns a profit and has PTI of 200 this year. Walk through the 3 financial statements assuming NOLs are used as a direct tax deduction on the financial statements

ii. Add back NOLs of 100 and call it Deferred Taxes
iii. Cash up by 40

ii. DTA s down by 100
iii. Asset side is down by 60

P/E * NI = Equity Value --> 4 * $200 = $800
EV = Equity Value + Debt + NCI – Cash = $800 + $200 + $75 - $50 = $1025.

Let’s say you have ParentCo, with 2 subs-CoffeeCo and DonutCo. You own 100% of CoffeeCo, and it has an EBITDA of 100m. CoffeeCo is private. You own 80% of DonutCo and it has an EBITDA of 200m. It also trades at 5x EBITDA. ParentCo has a share price of $10, with 100m shares. It has 500m in debt and 200m in cash. What multiple has the market implicitly assigned to CoffeeCo?
questions.answer:
a. ParentCo TEV = 10*100 + 500 – 200 = 1300
b. DonutCo TEV = 200*5 = 1000
c. CoffeeCo TEV = ParentCo TEV – DonutCo TEV = 1300 – 1000 = 300
d. 300 / 100 = 3x

questions.question: Company has 100 shares outstanding at a share price of 10 each. It has 10 options outstanding at an exercise price of 5 each. What is the diluted equity value?
questions.answer:
a. Basic equity value is 1000 bc 100 shares * 10 = 1000
b. The options outstanding are in the money bc the current share price is above the exercise price of 5
c. When options are exercised these 10 options becomes 10 shares
d. The number of shares becomes 110
e. The option proceeds are the 10 options * 5 exercise price therefore 50
f. Options proceeds / current share price equals repurchased shares therefore 50/10 =5
g. Diluted shares outstanding = shares outstanding + potential shares – shares repurchased or 100+10-5 or 105
h. Diluted equity value is 105 * 10 per share or 1050

questions.question: Do you include tax rate when calculating Enterprise value? What about the debt rate?
A company’s EV/EBITDA goes from 10x to 20x and EV/Sales goes from 2x to 4x. What is happening to the company and its EBITDA margins?
questions.answer: Relative to the company’s Enterprise Value, the company’s sales (revenue) has halved (2x to 4x). Its top-line has shrunk by 50%, as has EBITDA, so the company’s EBITDA margins have not changed, remaining at 20% (2x/10x --> 4x/20x).

questions.question: If two companies are trading at 8X EBITDA, one 100% Equity, one 50% Debt and 50% Equity… which has a higher P/E?
questions.answer: The company financed by 100% equity will have a higher P/E because the Equity Value is double that of the company funded partially by debt, and the impact of interest will not likely impact the valuation as heavily.

questions.question: A company is trading at 10x EV/LTM EBITDA, do you expect it to go up or down in the EV/NTM EBITDA multiple?
questions.answer: This would depend on the state of the company and the industry it belongs to, but generally you expect the multiple to fall. Most companies anticipate (and deliver on) growth in EBITDA while the numerator (Enterprise Value) is the present-day value and does not vary in either of these ratios. As a result, you expect the EV/NTM EBITDA multiple to be lower than 10x.

questions.question: Which is often higher - EV/EBITDA or EV/EBIT?
questions.answer: EV/EBIT will be often higher as EBIT should be lower than EBITDA.

questions.question: Two companies in the same industry trade at 10x and 7x EV/EBITDA - what could the cause of the difference?
questions.answer: Investors expects the company with the higher multiple to have greater growth prospects; therefore, they are willing to pay more for every $1 in EBITDA generated.

questions.question: What's the difference between EV/EBITDA and P/E? Which do you prefer?
questions.answer: EV/EBITDA is a multiple that is independent of capital structure, taxes, and depreciation/amortization; therefore, it is better for comparing companies with different leverage levels or ones that operate in different industries. One isn’t necessarily better than the other, it depends on the situation. For example, a P/E multiple may be more useful when valuing financial institutions where interest income is a core part of their business.

questions.question: A company has an EV/Sales of 2x and an EV/EBITDA of 8x, what is the EBITDA Margin? If the EV/EBIT is 16x, what industry could this company be in?
questions.answer: The EBITDA margin is 25%. Simply, take the reciprocal of EV/EBITDA, then multiply it by EV/Sales. EV will cancel out and you will be left with EBITDA/Sales = 2/8 which is 25%.

questions.question: One precedent transaction was 10x and the other was 5x, why is this the case?
questions.answer: Could be many reasons including different market conditions, one may be private, one may have greater growth prospects, etc.

questions.question: $100 in debt is issued, how does it impact your P/E and EV/EBITDA ratios?
questions.answer:
ASSUMING DEBT RAISED IS JUST CASH:
P/E ratio doesn’t change as Equity Value remains unchanged and the Earnings are identical EV/EBITDA doesn’t change because the additional cash cancels out the increase in debt ASSUMING DEBT IS SPENT ON A VALUE-GENERATING CAPITAL PROJECT:
P/E remains constant, but EV/EBITDA should increase as cash doesn’t change but Total Debt is increased

questions.question: How does a dividend impact your P/E, EV/EBITDA, and P/B ratio?
questions.answer:
P/E: Lower P/E
EV/EBITDA: No effect
P/B: Depends on my current P/B ratio. If it is 1, no change. Less than 1, lower. More than 1, higher.

questions.question: Net Income = 20, cash = 30, debt = 50, P/E = 11x, and EV/EBITDA = 8x. What’s the company’s EBITDA?
questions.answer:
Need to determine EV → EV = Equity Value + Debt – Cash
Equity Value = 11*20 = 220
So…EV = 220 + 50 – 30 = 240
EBITDA = 240/8 = 30

ii. 10 dollars in depreciation expense
iii. 80 in write-downs

questions.question: Why is debt less expensive than equity?
questions.answer:
a. Interest on debt is tax deductible through the tax shield
b. Debt is senior to equity in a firm's capital structure. In a liquidation or bankruptcy, the debt holders get paid first before the equity holders receive anything. To take on that additional risk, equity investor demand a superior return

questions.question: Company A buys company B with 100% debt. Company B has a PE multiple of 10x and Company A has PE multiple of 15x. What interest rate is required on the debt to make the deal dilutive?
questions.answer:
a. Company A Cost of Stock = 1/15 = 6.7%
b. Company B Yield = 1/10 = 10%
c. The after-tax cost of debt must be greater than 10% for the acquisition cost to exceed company b’s yield
d. 10%/(1-.4) = 16.7%
e. Would say approximately 17% interest rate on debt
f. Bc debt amount is high, the deal would probably be accretive

questions.question: Why do you fundamentally use P/E ratios as opposed to EV/EBITDA ratios?
questions.answer: If the capital structure is an integral part of the business, P/E would be a better ratio to use as apposed to EV/EBITDA. For example, financial institutions main source of income is interest which is important to include when valuing businesses within that industry

questions.question: You’re running a DCF on a biotech company and a consumer staples company both with the same WACC – which has a higher terminal value as a % of EV and why?
questions.answer: A biotech company is less mature and far less stable than a consumer staples company, and the high R&D expense likely reduces the amount of FCF it has throughout the holding period. Further, because these companies are valued for their growth potential, they trade at high multiples, so they would derive a greater portion of their EV from the TV than the consumer staples.

questions.question: What two ways do you use to get to a terminal value? Expand on what figures you use on each
questions.answer: Gordon Growth Method or Multiples Method. For the Multiples Method, we use comparable companies to determine an appropriate EV/EBITDA multiple. From there, we simply multiply our Terminal Year EBITDA by the Multiple to arrive at a Terminal Value. For the Gordon Growth Method, we will use a conservative growth rate (most likely in line with GDP growth, inflation, etc.) and use the perpetuity formula to determine a Terminal Value.

questions.question: What's the difference between DCF and DDM, walk me through both.
questions.answer: DCF is discounting UFCF or LFCF, while DDM’s valuation is based on future projected dividends. The models will mechanically work the same way.

questions.question: Why do you use Cost of Equity in a DDM?
questions.answer: In a Dividend Discount Model, rather than using the concept of free cash flow to value a business’ value creation, future proceeds are projected through dividends issued (a measured of the company’s “excess cash”). However, dividends are only attributable to equity holders, and therefore should be discounted at the opportunity cost for equity investors – the Cost of Equity.

questions.question: What are 3 things wrong with a DCF? (More are listed here)
questions.answer:
1. A considerable majority of the company’s value is placed on the terminal value (which is heavily reliant on assumptions, difficult to estimate and extremely sensitive to projections) (e.g. biotech companies)
2. Capital expenditure projections are typically presumed to be entirely maintenance-based and therefore do not represent accretion of company value through associated topline growth. It is therefore difficult to model specific growth opportunities in the future
3. General uncertainty and assumption levels: the entire model is built entirely on assumptions based on prior performance (from discount rate to growth rate)
4. Not applicable to business models that are balance-sheet centric (financial institutions, real estate / energy / mining)
5. Not very effective for cyclical businesses or businesses that have negative free cash flow

questions.question: NWC is steady in a DCF. How does an increase of XM of AR in Year X of a DCF affect FCF and valuation?
Does Revenue, COGS, or Capex impact a DCF the most? Why?
questions.answer: a. Capex, then COGS, then Revenue, b/c distance from FCF

questions.question: What determines how much a line item will affect a DCF?
questions.answer: a. Distance from the FCF line

questions.question: What will have a bigger impact on valuation, a 1% change to revenue growth or a 1% change to the discount rate? Why?
questions.answer: a. 1% change to discount rate, because it is closer to the bottom line of the DCF-

questions.question: If you change from LIFO to FIFO and costs are rising, how would this impact your DCF?
questions.answer: a. It wouldn’t, LIFO to FIFO would increase inventory value, but COGS goes down

questions.question: What happens to the PV of cash flows when using midyear convention?
questions.answer: a. Midyear convention moves each cash flow up by a half period which increases the PV since each CF is received earlier

questions.question: Explain the basic concept of a DCF.
questions.answer:
a. You value a company based on the PV of its FCFs far into the future
b. Divide the future into a near future period of 5-10 years
c. Calculate, project, discount and add those FCFs
d. Approximate the far future period FCFs
e. Discount far future period FCFs and discount to the present value
f. Add everything together

questions.question: How do you unlever beta?
questions.answer: a. Unlevered beta = levered beta / (1 + (1-tax rate)*(total debt/equity))

questions.question: Why do you un-lever and re-lever beta when you calculate it based on comps?
questions.answer:
a. Betas found online are already levered because company’s stock reflects debt take on
b. Bc each company has different cap structure, need to unlever it to determine a company’s riskiness regardless of debt to equity mix
c. You must relever the median unlevered beta to account for the cap structure and total risk of the company

questions.question: How would the risk free rate change during a crisis?
questions.answer: a. It would decrease because governments would drop interest rates to encourage spending

questions.question: How would beta change during a crisis?
questions.answer: a. Beta would increase due to increased volatility

questions.question: 2 identical companies. One has debt and one does not. Which has the higher WACC?
questions.answer: a. The one without debt will have a higher WACC bc debt is less expensive than equity

questions.question: How does you calculate the preferred stock % value of the WACC equation
questions.answer:
a. Go to 10Ks to find dividend paid out of preferred stock
b. Figure out how much preferred stock outstanding makes up the total capital structure
c. Divide the dividend by the price of the preferred stock to get the return

questions.question: Say you have two companies with same total enterprise value and trade at same multiples, but one is industrial, and one is pharmaceutical company, i.e. one has a much higher asset beta. Which one’s market cap would be higher?

Company A has EV of 100, market cap of 80, EBITDA of 10 and NI of 4. Company B has EV of 40, market cap of 40, EBITDA of 8 and NI of 2. Company A has 60 debt and 40 cash. Company A decided to acquire Company using 100% debt a 10% interest rate and 25% tax rate to acquire Company B. What are the combined multiples?
questions.answer:
a. Add market caps to get combined market caps of 120
b. Combined company has 40 additional debt therefore A has 60 Debt and 40 Cash. EV is 120+60+40-40 = 180
c. Combined EBITDA is 18 and EV/EBITDA = 180/18=10x
d. Interest expense on 40 debt at 10% interest is 4
e. 4*(1-.25) = 3
f. NI falls to 3
g. Combined PE = 120/3 = 40

questions.question: You have a target with an EV of $100 million and a debt/total cap of 60%, a 50% premium on the share price is given - what is the equity value of the firm? Let's say the company had $4 million in net income and the acquirer has a P/E of 15x, if it's an all stock deal, is it accretive or dilutive?
questions.answer: The equity value of the firm would be $60M. The deal would be neutral as both their P/E multiples would be 15x when considering the 50% premium we are placing on the share price.

questions.question: Follow up question to above - let's say the acquirer had net income of $10 million and shares outstanding of 10 million, is the acquisition accretive or dilutive to EPS?
questions.answer: Dilutive. Acquirer has a lower P/E than the target.

questions.question: Company A’s equity value is $200, has an EBIT of $100, tax rate of 50%, and a net income of $50. Company B’s P/E ratio is 4.5x. A acquires B in an all-stock deal, accretive or dilutive? Explain this is laymen terms
questions.answer:
Company A’s P/E: 200/50 = 4x → Dilutive
B trades higher relative to its earnings compared to A. Because of this, when we are acquiring company B in all- stock deal, we are essentially buying their earnings at a more expensive rate than what our shares are offering. Therefore, the deal is dilutive.

questions.question: Company has 10000 shares outstanding and a current share price of 20. It has 100 options outstanding at an exercise price of 10. It has 50 RSUs outstanding. It has 100 convertible bonds outstanding at a conversion price of 10 and a par value of 100.
questions.answer:
a. Options treatment
i. Bc the 100 options outstanding are in the money, they all get converted into 100 shares
ii. The company receives option proceeds of 100*10 = 1000
iii. Share price is 20 therefore it can repurchase 1000/20 = 50 shares with options proceeds
iv. There are now 50 shares outstanding bc 100 new shares – 50 repurchases = 50
b. RSU treatment – all 50 RSUs get added as if they’re common shares therefore there’s 100 shares outstanding again
c. Convertible bond treatment
i. Conversion price for convertible bonds is below company’s current share price so conversion is allowed
ii. Divide the par value by conversion price to see how many new shares per bond get created: 100/10 = 10 new shares per bond
iii. With 100 convertible bonds outstanding * 10 new shares per bond there are 1000 new shares
d. In total there are 1100 new shares between the options, RSUs and convertible bonds
e. Diluted share count is 10000+1100 = 11100 diluted shares outstanding
f. Diluted equity value is 11,000*20 or 222,000
